Vikas's diary, Tuesday night.
Told Zainab ma'am today that I'm leaving the studio at the end of March.
Last night I nearly backed out again, so I wrote four lines on an index card:
1. Thank you: for hiring me with no portfolio, for the Kochi project.
2. Decision: leaving end of March to join a friend's design firm.
3. Why: I want to try leading projects, and there's no opening here for two years.
4. Ask: can I finish the hotel project and help hire my replacement?
I didn't read it out. It stayed in my shirt pocket the whole time. But when she went quiet after point two and my mind went completely blank, I touched the card and remembered point three. That was enough to keep going.
She said she was sorry to lose me, and yes to the hotel project.

When I left my job to build a tuition-booking app, I had exactly nine months of savings. For the first two weeks I worked as if I had forever: fonts, a mascot, a pitch deck with animations.
Then one Sunday Urmila, who had agreed to be my co-founder, drew a line on a napkin. "Eshaan, month nine, you're broke. Raising money takes three months. So month six is the real deadline. What has to be true by month six for someone to invest?"
We argued, then agreed: two hundred parents who have booked and paid for a tutor at least twice. That was the proof.
After that, every task had to answer one question: does this get us closer to two hundred repeat bookings by month six? The mascot went. The animations went. Visits to three coaching centres got added. It felt harsh. It also felt like the first time I knew what I was doing.

subtype: Approach: weekly burn review with a kill threshold [Revision]
passage:
Wasim uncle stirred his tea and looked at his niece's pitch deck. "When Anjali and I started our tiffin delivery company, we were twenty-five and full of big talk. We had ten months of money. Every Friday, no matter what, we sat on the office floor with two numbers: what we spent that week, and how many customers signed up. And one rule written on the wall: if cash drops below four months and nobody is paying, we stop and change.
At month six it happened. Four months left, lots of free trials, not one paying customer. Anjali cried a little. I was angry. But we had promised the wall. We dropped the two paid delivery apps we used, let our freelance designer go, and spent the next weeks knocking on office doors ourselves with tiffins in our hands. The first paying customer was a bank branch. That rule saved us."

qa.q: What two numbers did they look at every Friday?
qa.a: What they spent that week, and how many customers signed up.

qa.q: What were Anjali and Wasim feeling when the rule was triggered?
qa.a: Anjali was upset enough to cry and Wasim was angry, but both kept their promise to the wall.

qa.q: Which choice in the story saved the company, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the Friday rule and switching to knocking on office doors, because it cut spending and put them face to face with buyers like the bank branch.

qa.q: How might the freelance designer have experienced being let go?
qa.a: The designer likely felt disappointed, but the decision came from a clear rule rather than a judgement about the designer's work.

grounding: It shows two young founders reviewing weekly spending against signups and, at four months of cash with no paying user, cutting paid tools and a freelancer to sell in person.
